sections.content: Memphis, Tennessee sits quietly in the shadows of flashier markets like Nashville and Atlanta — and that's exactly why savvy investors love it. Real estate deals in Memphis TN offer some of the best price-to-rent ratios in the entire Southeast, with median home prices well below the national average and rental demand that stays strong year-round. Whether you're a seasoned wholesaler, a first-time flipper, or a buy-and-hold landlord building long-term wealth, Memphis deserves a serious look. If you're just getting started, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide before diving in — it'll give you a solid foundation for everything we cover here.
Memphis Market Overview: Why Investors Keep Coming Back

Memphis is the largest city in Tennessee by population, home to roughly 633,000 residents within city limits and about 1.3 million in the greater metro area. The city's economy runs on logistics, healthcare, and manufacturing. FedEx is headquartered here, and Memphis is one of the busiest cargo airports in the world. That economic engine creates steady employment, which translates directly into rental demand for investors. The city also has a large percentage of renters — roughly 54% of households rent rather than own — which is excellent news if you're building a rental portfolio. You can explore current property data and deal opportunities on our dedicated [Memphis, TN market page](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/memphis-tn) to get a real-time picture of what's available right now.
Average Home Prices and What Your Money Gets You

The median home price in Memphis hovers around $165,000 to $185,000 as of late 2024, depending on the data source and neighborhood. Compare that to the national median of roughly $420,000 and you start to see the opportunity. Distressed properties — the bread and butter of wholesalers and flippers — can be found in the $40,000 to $90,000 range, with after-repair values (ARV) often landing between $120,000 and $200,000 depending on location and renovation quality. That spread creates real room for profit. Rental properties in desirable mid-tier neighborhoods typically rent for $900 to $1,400 per month, giving investors gross rent-to-price ratios that often exceed 1% — a benchmark many cash-flow investors target. Use our free [ARV Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/arv-calculator) to quickly estimate after-repair value on any Memphis property before you make an offer.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Memphis

Memphis is a tale of many zip codes. Some areas carry high crime and low appreciation potential, while others are quietly transforming into landlord goldmines. Here's a breakdown of neighborhoods worth targeting based on your investment strategy.
For Buy-and-Hold Rentals

items: Frayser: One of the most affordable entry points in the city. Cash flow is strong, though tenant screening is critical. Home prices often start below $70,000.
Raleigh: A working-class neighborhood with steady rental demand and improving infrastructure. Good for Section 8 investors.
Hickory Hill: Mid-tier suburb with strong rental demand from working families. Homes typically range from $90,000 to $150,000.
Whitehaven: Southern Memphis neighborhood with consistent tenant base and decent price-to-rent ratios. Known as a solid landlord market.
Cordova: Eastern suburb with higher-quality tenants, better schools, and newer housing stock. Lower cap rates but lower headaches too.

sections.content: For Fix-and-Flip Opportunities

items: Midtown Memphis: Gentrifying rapidly. Craftsman bungalows and Victorian homes can be bought distressed and flipped to young professionals for $180,000–$250,000.
Cooper-Young: Trendy, walkable, artsy. Renovated homes here command premium prices and sell fast.
Binghampton: Up-and-coming area with growing demand. Entry prices are still low enough for strong flip margins.
South Memphis: High risk but high reward for experienced investors willing to do their homework on comps.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Before buying in any Memphis neighborhood, pull crime statistics from the Memphis Police Department's online crime map and cross-reference with vacancy rates. High vacancy in a neighborhood is often a red flag that rental demand isn't as strong as it looks on paper.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Memphis
Wholesaling

Memphis is a wholesaler's market. The high volume of distressed, vacant, and absentee-owned properties creates a steady pipeline of motivated sellers. Typical wholesale assignment fees in Memphis range from $5,000 to $20,000, with some deals going higher in hot pockets like Midtown. The key is finding motivated sellers before they hit the MLS — which means direct mail, driving for dollars, probate leads, and tax-delinquent lists. If you're new to this strategy, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide walks you through every step of the process. Once you have a deal under contract, run the numbers through our [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to make sure your buyer has room to profit before you assign it.
Fix and Flip

Flipping in Memphis can be very profitable if you control your renovation costs tightly. Labor is relatively affordable compared to coastal markets, and material costs are in line with national averages. A typical flip in Midtown or Cooper-Young might look like this: purchase price $75,000, renovation budget $45,000, total investment $120,000 plus carrying costs, and an ARV of $195,000. That's a rough gross profit of $75,000 before agent fees and holding costs — not bad. The risk? Scope creep and inexperienced contractors. Always get multiple bids and use a licensed general contractor with Memphis-specific experience.
Long-Term Rentals and Section 8

Memphis has one of the largest Section 8 housing voucher programs in Tennessee. For buy-and-hold investors, this can mean guaranteed monthly rent payments directly from the government, lower vacancy risk, and tenants who tend to stay long-term once established. Section 8 rents in Memphis are set by the Housing Authority's payment standards, which for a 3-bedroom unit currently run around $1,050 to $1,350 per month. If you buy a 3-bedroom in Whitehaven or Raleigh for $90,000, you're potentially looking at a 12–14% gross rent yield — far above what most markets offer.
Memphis Real Estate Market Trends for 2024

The Memphis market has remained relatively stable even as higher interest rates squeezed buyers in more expensive cities. Because home prices are lower, the affordability impact of rate increases is less severe. Here are the key trends shaping deals right now: inventory remains tight but slightly better than 2022 peaks; days on market have increased from an average of 18 days in 2021 to closer to 45–60 days in 2024, giving investors more negotiating leverage; and investor activity remains high, with out-of-state buyers from California, Illinois, and New York continuing to target Memphis for cash-flow properties. One trend worth watching is the continued expansion of the medical district and Crosstown Concourse area, which is driving appreciation in adjacent neighborhoods.

"Memphis is the kind of market where you don't have to hit home runs. You can make money on singles and doubles all day long because the entry prices are so low and the rental demand never really goes away." — Common sentiment among experienced Memphis buy-and-hold investors
Practical Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Memphis

Investing remotely in Memphis is very common — many of the city's landlords live out of state. But doing it successfully requires a specific game plan. Learning [how to find off-market real estate deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) remotely is one of the most important skills you can develop, and it applies directly to the Memphis market where the best opportunities rarely hit Zillow.

items: Build your team first: You need a local property manager, a reliable inspector, and a contractor before you buy your first deal. Interview at least three of each.
Never skip the inspection: Memphis has a lot of older housing stock. Foundation issues, HVAC problems, and knob-and-tube wiring are common. A $400 inspection can save you $40,000.
Use a property management company from day one: Remote landlords who self-manage Memphis properties often struggle with tenant issues and local code compliance. A good PM runs 8–10% of monthly rent.
Understand Memphis-specific landlord-tenant laws: Tennessee law is generally landlord-friendly, but Memphis has local ordinances around habitability standards and eviction procedures.
Visit before you scale: Spend two or three days on the ground before buying your third or fourth property. Walking neighborhoods in person reveals things Google Street View never will.

Analyze deals thoroughly: Use data-driven tools to run your numbers before making offers. Knowing how to [analyze real estate deals like a pro](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals) will keep you from buying a property that looks good on paper but bleeds cash in reality.

sections.content: Pro Tip: When evaluating Memphis rentals, always budget 10% for vacancy, 10% for repairs and maintenance, and 10% for property management — even if you plan to self-manage at first. If the deal still cash flows after those reserves, you have a real deal. If it doesn't, keep looking.
